chapter_title: The VM Translator: Implementing Function Calling

screens.title: Implementing Function Calling in the VM Translator
screens.subtitle: How the translator creates and restores call frames, initializes locals, and boots the VM.

narration.text: In this chapter you will complete the VM translator's function-calling machinery. You will learn how the translator converts VM commands into assembly that saves the caller's context, establishes a new frame for the callee, and returns a result to the caller. We will also generate bootstrap code that initializes the stack pointer and calls the operating system initializer, and support multiple VM files so static variables and symbols are handled globally. Through concrete assembly templates and careful stack-frame reasoning you will see why each step matters: pushing a return address, saving LCL, ARG, THIS, and THAT, computing ARG = SP - nArgs - 5, and restoring the caller's frame on return. You will practice with test programs that exercise simple calls, nested calls, and recursive calls like Fibonacci. By the end, you'll be able to implement function, call, and return, add bootstrap code, concatenate multiple files, and test the translator end-to-end. Consider: what happens if the return address is not preserved? That single mistake breaks the entire call chain.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Function calling is stack manipulation: save caller state, set up callee frame with locals, jump, then restore and return value.

content.html:

Function calling mechanics

This slide introduces the pieces you will implement: the function command that creates locals, the call and return sequences that save and restore frames, and the bootstrap that starts the VM. Understanding these pieces is essential to translating higher-level VM programs into working assembly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will implement three VM commands and the bootstrap sequence, handle multiple VM files, and run end-to-end tests. First, you will translate the function command to assembly that creates a labeled entry and pushes n local zeros so each function has its own local space. Second, you will implement call by pushing a return address and caller state and by computing ARG correctly so the callee finds its arguments. Third, you will implement return by restoring the caller's frame pointers and moving the return value back to the caller's stack position. You will also add bootstrap code that sets the stack pointer to 256 and invokes the operating system initializer, Sys. init, so programs run in a properly configured environment. Finally, you will test with SimpleFunction, NestedCall, FibonacciElement, StaticsTest, and Pong to ensure correctness across recursion, nesting, and multiple files. These skills are essential for building a correct VM-to-assembly translator.

keyIdea.text: Translate function/call/return, bootstrap the VM, support multiple files, and validate with the provided test programs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Tests
screens.subtitle: How to validate your implementation and what to check

narration.text: Testing is part of the objective. You will validate your function-calling implementation with example programs that exercise local allocation, nested calls, recursion, and static variables shared across files. For each test program you should inspect the generated assembly for correct labels, return address uniqueness, ARG calculation, and proper SP updates. Run SimpleFunction to see a single call and local allocation. Use NestedCall to check multiple nested frames and ensure restoration of caller pointers. Use FibonacciElement to exercise recursion and to practice tracing call frames and stack depth. StaticsTest checks that static variables are allocated and referenced consistently across files. Pong is a full integration test that relies on correct bootstrap and OS initialization. As you test, use the C P U Emulator to step through the assembly, observe SP changes, and verify that returns land at the saved return address. These validations will expose common bugs like off-by-five in ARG or failing to restore LCL.

keyIdea.title: Testing focus
keyIdea.text: Validate frame prologue/epilogue, ARG computation, return address uniqueness, and global static allocation across concatenated files.

  • • LCL updated to SP after pushing saved context and return address.
  • • On return, THAT, THIS, ARG, LCL restored from the saved frame in the correct order.
  • • Static variables emitted with global names and not reallocated per file.

screens.title: What function calling means in the VM translator
screens.subtitle: A clear definition of frames, caller/callee responsibilities, and why we need saved pointers

narration.text: Function calling in the VM translator is a disciplined sequence of stack and pointer manipulations that allow nested and recursive code to run without corrupting values. At its core a function call changes control flow and creates a new frame: the caller saves its return address and important segment pointers, then transfers control to the callee which establishes its own local storage. When the callee finishes, it returns a value and restores the caller's frame so execution resumes exactly where it left off. A common mental model is a stack of hotel rooms: each call gets a room with its own locals, and the caller's room is locked and remembered until the callee checks out. This model explains why we push LCL, ARG, THIS, and THAT before jumping; those pointers describe the caller's room and must be restored later. A misconception to avoid is thinking that only the return address matters; failing to save pointers loses the caller's locals and argument base. As a concrete example, consider a function that calls a helper which overwrites THIS: if THIS is not saved, the caller cannot access its object data after the helper returns. The takeaway is that saving and restoring the full frame is essential for correct nested and recursive behavior.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A function call creates a new stack frame, preserving caller state and giving the callee private locals and argument access.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › What function calling means
Definition

Frame-based call semantics

A frame is the caller's saved context plus the callee's locals and arguments. The translator implements this by pushing values onto the stack and updating pointer registers so both caller and callee find their data reliably.

Analogy: hotel rooms
Caller packs its state, leaves a return address, and the callee sets up its room with zeroed locals. On return the caller's room is restored.
Common misconception
Only saving the return address is insufficient; local pointers must be preserved too or the caller loses its address bases.
Visual
Stack frame layout
Top of stack: caller pushes return address, then LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT. After that the callee will set ARG and LCL and push its locals. On return the saved frame is used to restore pointers and to retrieve the return address.
Key Takeaway

Successful calls require both a saved return address and saved frame pointers to preserve caller context across nested and recursive calls.

screens.title: Implementing the function command
screens.subtitle: Emit label and push n local zeros onto the stack

narration.text: The function command creates a labeled entry point and allocates space for local variables by pushing zeros. The VM command has the form: function functionName nLocals. The correct assembly sequence begins with a label for the function entry and then loops nLocals times to push 0 onto the stack, incrementing SP each time. This ensures each local variable slot is initialized, avoiding garbage values. A concrete implementation pattern uses a counter in the D register and a loop label that writes 0 to *SP, increments SP, decrements the counter, and repeats until zero. A common mistake is to forget to update SP after writing the zero, which leaves SP pointing at the last stored zero and corrupts the subsequent push logic. Another pitfall is miscomputing the loop bounds when nLocals is zero; the translator should emit no loop instructions in that case and simply place the function label. When you test, check the generated assembly for the function label and the correct loop structure, and run the C P U Emulator to watch SP grow by nLocals at function entry. Can you see how initializing locals avoids unpredictable behavior in nested calls?

keyIdea.title: Function prologue
keyIdea.text: Emit a function label then push nLocals zeros to ensure deterministic local slots and correct SP advancement.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Implementing the function command
Code walkthrough

Assembly template for function

(functionName)     // Function entry label
// Push nLocals zeros onto the stack
@nLocals
D=A
(LOOP)
@END_LOCALS
D;JEQ
@SP
A=M
M=0
@SP
M=M+1
D=D-1
@LOOP
0;JMP
(END_LOCALS)
This sequence creates a label, sets D to nLocals, then loops writing zero at RAM[SP] and incrementing SP until D reaches zero. If nLocals is zero the loop exits immediately.
Explanation
  • • The label is the function entry point used by calls to jump into this code.
  • • Initializing locals to zero makes variable behavior deterministic across runs.
  • • The loop uses D as a counter so the implementation avoids extra temporary memory if nLocals is small.
  • • Edge case: emit only the label when nLocals is 0; no loop code is needed.
Common mistake

Forgetting to update SP after storing zero leaves the stack pointer stale and corrupts future pushes and frame math.

screens.title: Implementing the call command
screens.subtitle: Push return address and caller state; compute ARG and LCL; jump to callee

narration.text: The call command performs several ordered steps that establish the callee's frame and preserve the caller. When you translate call functionName nArgs, follow a clear process. First, push a unique return address and increment SP. Next, push the current values of LCL, ARG, THIS, and THAT — these are the caller's frame pointers. Each push increments SP so the saved frame sits on the stack above the return address. Then compute ARG = SP - nArgs - 5; this positions ARG so the callee's argument 0 maps to the caller-supplied topmost argument. After setting ARG, set LCL = SP so the callee can use LCL-based addressing for its locals. Finally, jump to the function label and place the return label after the call so execution continues there when the callee returns. A concrete example: if SP is 300 and nArgs is 2, ARG becomes 300 - 2 - 5 = 293; the callee will find its arguments at R A M[293..]. A frequent bug is miscomputing the -5 offset; forgetting these five saved slots (return address, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT) shifts ARG and breaks argument addressing. The takeaway: call must both save the caller and compute the callee's base correctly.

keyIdea.title: Call sequence
keyIdea.text: Push return address and saved pointers, set ARG = SP - nArgs - 5, set LCL = SP, then jump to the function label.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Implementing the call command
Process

Step-by-step call prologue

  1. Push a unique return address and increment SP.
  2. Push LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT in that order, each time incrementing SP.
  3. Compute ARG = SP - nArgs - 5 and store it in ARG.
  4. Set LCL = SP.
  5. Jump to functionName and place the return label after the jump.
Example
If SP=300 and nArgs=2 then ARG becomes 293, so the callee finds its two arguments beginning at RAM[293] and a clean region for local allocation above SP.
Assembly pattern
// Push return address
@RET_LABEL
D=A
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1

// Push LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT
@LCL
D=M
@SP
A=M
M=D
@SP
M=M+1
// (repeat for ARG, THIS, THAT)

// ARG = SP - nArgs - 5
@SP
D=M
@nArgs
D=D-A
@5
D=D-A
@ARG
M=D

// LCL = SP
@SP
D=M
@LCL
M=D

// Jump to function
@functionName
0;JMP

(RET_LABEL)
Ensure RET_LABEL is unique per call. A translator typically generates labels with an increasing counter to avoid collisions across files and calls.

screens.title: Implementing the return command
screens.subtitle: Restore the saved frame, reposition SP, and jump to the return address

narration.text: The return command reverses the call sequence: it must restore the caller's frame pointers, move the callee's return value into the caller's expected location, reset SP, and jump to the saved return address. A robust return implementation follows a small frame protocol. First save the return value at the top of the stack into a temporary register so it is safe while we restore pointers. Then compute a frame pointer, typically stored in a temporary register like R13, where frame = LCL. Using offsets from frame restore THAT, THIS, ARG, and LCL by fetching frame - 1, frame - 2, and so on. After restoring the pointers, set SP = ARG + 1 so the stack pointer points just after the caller's arguments. Copy the return value from the temporary register into R A M[ARG] so the caller sees the returned value at its argument 0. Finally jump to the saved return address stored in another temporary like R13 or R14 and transfer control back to the caller. A common misconception is to write the return value directly without adjusting SP; if SP is not reset first, the caller's stack layout will be wrong. When testing, ensure the callee places the return value in ARG and that the caller's SP and registers are preserved across return.

keyIdea.title: Return epilogue
keyIdea.text: Save return value, restore THAT/THIS/ARG/LCL from the saved frame, set SP = ARG + 1, write return to ARG, and jump to return address.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Implementing the return command
Code walkthrough
// Save return value in temp
@SP
A=M-1
D=M
@R14
M=D

// Restore THAT, THIS, ARG, LCL
@LCL
D=M
@R13
M=D
// ... (restore segment pointers from the saved frame)

// Set SP = ARG + 1
@ARG
D=M+1
@SP
M=D

// Push return value
@R14
D=M
@SP
A=M-1
M=D

// Jump to return address
@R13
A=M
0;JMP
The pattern uses temporary registers for the frame and return value. Restoring pointers uses offsets from the saved frame address so each pointer returns to its caller value.
Explanation & checklist
  • • Save return value before modifying SP or restoring pointers.
  • • Compute frame = LCL and use frame offsets to restore THAT, THIS, ARG, LCL.
  • • Set SP = ARG + 1 so the caller's stack layout is correct.
  • • Place return value at RAM[ARG] and jump to saved return address.
Debug hint

If returns land at the wrong place, verify the return-label generation and that the saved return address wasn't overwritten during the callee's execution.

screens.title: Bootstrap code: initializing the VM
screens.subtitle: Set SP = 256 and call Sys.init to start the program

narration.text: Bootstrap code gives the generated assembly a correct starting state. The translator must emit instructions at the beginning of the output file to initialize the stack pointer and then transfer control to the operating system's entry point. Specifically, set SP to 256 so that the stack starts in R A M above the fixed memory areas, then invoke Sys. init, which performs OS-level setup and eventually calls Main. main. The bootstrap sequence is short but critical: without it programs that depend on OS services or global allocation will fail. The assembly template sets R A M[SP] to 256 and then jumps to the Sys. init label. An important subtlety is that Sys. init must exist or be provided by the program and OS VM code; the translator only emits the call to it. Another common misconception is calling Main. main directly; Sys. init is the agreed entry point so the OS can prepare resources before handing control to user code. When testing, ensure bootstrap appears once at the top of the generated. asm file and that subsequent file concatenation does not re-emit bootstrap code for each. vm file. The key takeaway is that a correct bootstrap establishes a consistent runtime starting state for all translated programs.

keyIdea.title: Bootstrap
keyIdea.text: Emit SP = 256 and call Sys.init once at the start of the assembly file to initialize the runtime environment.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Bootstrap code
Assembly
// Initialize SP = 256
@256
D=A
@SP
M=D

// Call Sys.init (the OS entry point)
@Sys.init
0;JMP
Place this code once at the top of the generated assembly file. It sets up a consistent stack base and transfers control to the OS initializer.
Why Sys.init
Sys.init performs system initialization such as allocator and device setup, then calls user code. Calling it ensures the environment is ready before Main.main executes. Emitting bootstrap more than once or in the wrong place leads to duplicate initialization and unexpected behavior.
Key Takeaway

Bootstrap sets SP and invokes Sys.init exactly once; do not emit it per input file when translating a directory of VM files.

screens.title: Stack frames: concrete layout and addresses
screens.subtitle: How return address and saved pointers are organized on the stack

narration.text: A concrete view of the stack frame clarifies the arithmetic used during calls and returns. When a caller performs a call, it pushes these items in order: the return address, then LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT. After these five pushes, the callee sets ARG = SP - nArgs - 5 and LCL = SP. Locals are then pushed by the callee, growing the stack above LCL. Visualize memory growing upward: the return address sits below the saved pointers, and ARG points into the caller's argument region below the saved frame. On return, using frame = LCL, offsets are applied to retrieve saved pointers: THAT = *(frame - 1), THIS = *(frame - 2), ARG = *(frame - 3), LCL = *(frame - 4) if you consider the frame pointer arithmetic accordingly. A typical implementation stores frame in a temporary register and reads these offsets to restore the caller state. A practical example: if a caller had SP=300, after pushing return and four pointers SP becomes 305; after callee pushes its locals SP increases further. When returning, restoring pointers from frame avoids recomputing their values from scratch. Misunderstanding these offsets leads to restoring incorrect pointers and corrupting the caller environment. The key insight: consistent offsets and ordering guarantee that every saved value is retrievable in the correct sequence.

keyIdea.title: Frame layout
keyIdea.text: Order the saved values: return address, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT. Use frame = LCL and fixed offsets to restore them on return.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Stack frames
Annotated layout
Stack snapshot (low addr at bottom)
return-address ← saved return address
saved LCL
saved ARG
saved THIS
saved THAT
arg0 (caller-supplied)
arg1
...
local0 (callee)
Use frame = LCL to access saved pointers with fixed negative offsets. Restoring THEM in order is what returns the VM to the caller's context.
Practical checklist
  • • Confirm the push order when emitting call code matches the expected restore offsets.
  • • Save frame = LCL into a temp register before restoring values.
  • • Restore pointers from frame - 1, frame - 2, etc., according to the template you implement.
  • • After restoring, reset SP = ARG + 1 so caller's stack area is intact.
Why ordering matters

A different push order would require different offsets on restore. The standard chosen ordering makes ARG calculation and restore code straightforward and consistent across calls.

screens.title: Unique labels and return-address generation
screens.subtitle: How to create safe return labels across files and calls

narration.text: Return addresses must be unique so that when a callee returns control, execution continues at the correct point. The translator therefore generates labels for return addresses that include a call-site-unique counter and optionally the file or function name. For example, a translator might emit RET_label0, RET_label1, or ClassName$ret. Using a global counter avoids collisions across functions and across input files when concatenated into a single. asm output. A common design is to increment a counter each time the translator emits a call and embed that counter in the return label. A trap to avoid is reusing labels when translating multiple files: if you reset the counter per-file, you risk collisions when concatenating outputs. Another possible source of collision is using function names alone; if two call sites target the same callee, their return points must still be different. A safe strategy is to include both the caller identity and a unique integer. As a concrete example, when translating a directory of VM files, maintain a translator-level counter that persists across files to guarantee global uniqueness. The takeaway: unique return labels are essential for correct returns in nested and recursive calls, especially when multiple files are translated into one assembly file.

keyIdea.title: Label uniqueness
keyIdea.text: Generate return labels using a global counter and optional file/function context so labels never collide across calls or files.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Unique labels

Strategies for return labels

• Global counter: RET.0, RET.1, RET.2 — incremented each call, never reset per-file.
• Contextual labels: FileName$RET0 or FunctionName$RET0 — embeds caller context for readability.
• Combined approach: FileName$RET0 where RET0 is global counter ensures both uniqueness and traceability.
Pitfall

Resetting a counter for each file will create duplicate labels after concatenation. Keep counters at translator scope, not file scope.

Example
@RET_42 D=A @SP A=M M=D @SP M=M+1
This shows a call pushing a uniquely named return label. The translator should ensure @RET_42 is unique by using a global counter.
Key Takeaway

Use a translator-global counter or include file context so every call site gets a distinct return label across concatenated files.

screens.title: Handling multiple VM files and static variables
screens.subtitle: Concatenate translations and allocate static variables globally

narration.text: When the translator receives a directory of VM files, it must translate each file and concatenate the results into a single assembly file. This requires consistent naming for static variables and labels so symbols from different files do not clash. The simple rule is to qualify static variables with the originating file name, for example FileName. index, and to ensure that these names are used consistently whenever static segment accesses are generated. Doing so provides global allocation semantics: the same static name maps to a single assembly symbol shared by all functions and files. Also be careful not to emit bootstrap code multiple times; the bootstrap sequence belongs once at the very beginning of the output file. File processing order matters only insofar as the translator must preserve consistent label generation and symbol naming. A practical test is StaticsTest: run it and inspect that a static variable written in one VM file is correctly read by another. A common mistake is to create per-file static pools that accidentally shadow each other after concatenation. To avoid this, use file-qualified names for statics and maintain global counters or registries for any labels that must be unique across all files. The takeaway: treat the output assembly as a single program and manage symbol visibility at the translator level, not per-file.

keyIdea.title: Multiple-file handling
keyIdea.text: Translate all files into one assembly, qualify static names by file, and emit bootstrap only once at the file start.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Multiple VM files

Symbol scoping

• Qualify static symbols with the file name: FileName.0, FileName.1, etc.
• Treat the concatenated assembly as a single program; avoid per-file bootstrap emission.
• Maintain translator-global counters for unique labels across all input files.
Example check

In StaticsTest, a static variable set in A.vm should be visible when read in B.vm because both reference A.index as the same assembly symbol.

Concatenation order

Translate files in a deterministic order (for example, alphabetical) so the output is reproducible. But correctness depends on symbol naming and label uniqueness, not the specific file order.

Key Takeaway

Use file-qualified static names and translator-level unique label generation to keep the assembled program correct when merging multiple VM translations.

screens.title: Testing the complete VM translator
screens.subtitle: How to validate using the provided example programs

narration.text: Testing the function-calling implementation involves running the translated assembly for each provided example and checking both functional behavior and internal stack correctness. Start with SimpleFunction to verify that a single call and the function prologue push the correct number of zeros for locals and that the return lands at the expected label. Next run NestedCall to exercise stacked frames; step through calls and returns in the C P U Emulator and watch that LCL, ARG, THIS, and THAT are correctly restored in order. Use FibonacciElement to test recursion: it verifies that the call/return code supports deep nesting and that saved pointers are not corrupted across recursive invocations. For StaticsTest, ensure that static variables are shared globally across files by inspecting symbol names in the assembly output. Finally, run Pong for full integration to ensure the bootstrap code and OS initialization worked and that the game runs end-to-end. When debugging, check for common errors: off-by-five in ARG computation, failing to increment SP after writing zeros for locals, return labels colliding, or emitting bootstrap code multiple times. Use the C P U Emulator's step and memory inspect features to measure SP adjustments and to trace where returns jump. Conclude each test by asking: did the caller's local and argument values survive a nested call unchanged? That question confirms correctness.

keyIdea.title: Testing flow
keyIdea.text: Use the sample programs to check prologue/epilogue correctness, static scoping, label uniqueness, and bootstrap behavior via the CPU Emulator.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Testing the translator

Test sequence

  1. SimpleFunction: check local allocation and single return.
  2. NestedCall: step through stacked frames and pointer restoration.
  3. FibonacciElement: verify recursion and max stack depth behavior.
  4. StaticsTest: confirm shared static variables across files.
  5. Pong: full integration with bootstrap and OS services.
Debugger tips

Use single-step and memory inspection to watch SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT change on each call and return. Track return label targets to ensure uniqueness.

Hands-on questions

• How many stack frames are created when computing fib(5)? Trace calls to count frames.
• What is the maximum stack depth during Fibonacci recursion? Use the emulator to measure SP.
• How many assembly instructions are generated for the Fibonacci VM code? Inspect the output file and count instructions.
Reflective prompt

If a test fails, which part of the call sequence would you check first: return address handling, ARG math, or frame restoration? Choose and justify.

screens.title: Tracing Fibonacci: counting frames and instructions
screens.subtitle: A guided approach to trace recursion and measure stack behavior

narration.text: Tracing recursive programs like Fibonacci gives you insight into how frames accumulate and how deep the stack grows. Start by translating fib(n) into assembly and then instrument a small trace: run the program in the C P U Emulator and mark each call and return. Each call to fib pushes a return address and the saved pointers, then creates locals. For fib(5) you can reason about the recursion tree: each call to fib(k) for k>1 produces two recursive calls fib(k-1) and fib(k-2). To count frames, follow the call tree: fib(5) produces a set number of calls equal to the number of nodes in the recursion tree. The stack depth at any moment equals the longest path from root to a leaf, so the maximum depth for fib(5) corresponds to the longest chain of nested calls. Practically, use the emulator's memory watch on SP and record its maximum. To count instructions executed, run the emulator and use its cycle counter or step count to measure instructions between program start and termination. A typical debugging pattern is to annotate calls with unique return labels so you can search the assembly and reason about how many call sequences are emitted. Misconceptions to avoid: counting total calls vs counting unique frames — recursive calls create many frames, some with identical code but distinct runtime frames. The closing question: after tracing, did the maximum SP match your theoretical longest call chain?

keyIdea.title: Trace method
keyIdea.text: Measure maximum SP in the emulator to find stack depth and step count to measure instruction execution for recursive calls.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Tracing Fibonacci

Tracing steps

  1. Translate fib VM into assembly with unique return labels per call site.
  2. Run in CPU Emulator and watch SP at each call to record maximum value.
  3. Count call events to measure how many frames were created during execution.
  4. Use the emulator's instruction counter to measure executed instructions for the whole run.
Practical hint

Annotate the VM code with comments where calls occur so the generated assembly contains identifiable call-site labels to search and count emitted call prologues and epilogues.

Example question

• How many stack frames are created when computing fib(5)? Trace calls to count frames in the emulator.
• What is the maximum stack depth? Record SP and subtract base SP to compute depth.
• How many assembly instructions are executed? Use the emulator's cycle/instruction counter.
Reflection

Comparing measured counts with your theoretical call-tree counts helps you understand the cost of recursion and validates that your translator emits prologues and epilogues correctly for every call.

screens.title: Debugging tips and common pitfalls
screens.subtitle: What typically goes wrong and how to fix it

narration.text: Several recurring bugs appear when implementing function calling; knowing them helps you debug fast. First, off-by-five errors in ARG computation are common: ARG must be SP - nArgs - 5 because five items were pushed before computing ARG: return address, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT. If you forget the 5, argument references inside the callee point to wrong memory. Second, failing to increment SP after pushing zeros for locals results in SP pointing to the last written zero rather than the next free slot. Third, overwriting the saved return address within the callee will cause returns to jump to the wrong address; use unique return labels and avoid writing to the memory locations where you stored the return address. Fourth, emitting bootstrap code multiple times when translating a directory breaks initialization; place bootstrap once at the top of the combined assembly. When debugging, instrument the translator to emit comments around each call and return sequence and use the C P U Emulator to step through those regions. Verify SP changes after each push/pop and confirm restored LCL/ARG values match their saved values. Finally, test statics across files to ensure consistent naming. The guided question to end: which of these errors would cause immediate crashes versus subtle incorrect results? Understanding their impact helps prioritize fixes.

keyIdea.title: Debug list
keyIdea.text: Watch for ARG off-by-five, missing SP increments for locals, overwritten return addresses, duplicate bootstrap emission, and inconsistent static naming.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.2 › Debugging tips

Common pitfalls

  • • ARG off-by-five: ensure ARG = SP - nArgs - 5.
  • • Missing SP increment after pushing locals.
  • • Return address overwritten during callee execution.
  • • Duplicate bootstrap emitted per file.
  • • Static names colliding across files.

Fixes & checks

• Add assertions in the translator for ARG calculation and SP updates.
• Emit translator-level comments around prologue/epilogue for easy emulator stepping.
• Keep a global counter for return labels and never reset per file.
• Qualify static names with file name to avoid collisions.
Key Takeaway

Systematic checks on SP movement and saved frame values catch most implementation errors quickly during emulator runs.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact memory cards for quick revision

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas you must retain. First, the call sequence: pushing a unique return address and saving LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT preserves the caller's context. Second, the callee's prologue and epilogue: allocate locals by pushing zeros, compute ARG correctly as SP - nArgs - 5, set LCL, and on return restore frame pointers and place the return value at ARG. Third, bootstrap and multi-file handling: emit SP = 256 and call Sys. init once, qualify static names by the file to preserve global static allocation, and generate globally unique labels across all files. Keep testing in your workflow: SimpleFunction, NestedCall, FibonacciElement, StaticsTest, and Pong each check different aspects of the implementation. These compact principles together ensure that nested and recursive functions execute correctly and that the translator produces reliable assembly for the entire program.

keyIdea.text: Call/save/restore, prologue/epilogue correctness, and bootstrap plus global symbol management.

Call & Save
Push return address and save LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT so the caller's context is preserved.
Prologue & Return
Function label + push n locals; on return restore frame and place return value at ARG.
Bootstrap & Files
Emit SP=256, call Sys.init once, and qualify static symbols across concatenated files.
Summary: correct push/pop ordering, ARG math, returning the value to ARG, and globally-unique labels are the pieces that make the VM translator's function calling reliable.

screens.title: What to Remember — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three concise reminders for implementation and testing

narration.text: Keep three quick reminders in mind while implementing and testing. First, ARG must be computed as SP - nArgs - 5; that -5 is not optional. Second, always save and later restore LCL, ARG, THIS, and THAT in the order your implementation assumes; consistency between save and restore is what allows correct returns. Third, when processing multiple files, qualify static symbols and use a translator-global counter for return labels so concatenated assembly remains collision-free. These short checks guide both implementation and debugging, letting you quickly find the source of incorrect returns or corrupted locals during emulator runs. What to Remember — Quick Reference means arg = sp - nargs - 5; save/restore lcl/arg/this/that consistently; use global naming for statics and return labels.. In practical terms, three concise reminders for implementation and testing. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
